::: remark

The sample mean of many independent random variables,
none of which dominates the others,
has a distribution that is approximately bell-shaped,
whatever the distributions of the individual variables.
@thm-clt makes this precise.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-clt}
#### Central Limit Theorem

Let $X_1, X_2, \ldots$ be [IID](independence.qmd#def-iid) random variables
with population mean $\mean$ and finite variance $\ss > 0$,
and let $\samplemean{X}{n} \eqdef \avgin X_i$.
Then for every real number $z$
[@wikipedia_central_limit_theorem]:

$$
\lim_{n \to \infty} \Prf{\frac{\sqrt{n}\,(\samplemean{X}{n} - \mean)}{\sdpar} \le z} = \normcdf(z)
$$

where $\normcdf(z) \eqdef \int_{-\infty}^{z} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \text{e}^{-u^2/2}\,du$
is the CDF of the [standard normal distribution](random-variables.qmd#def-std-normal) $\ndist{0, 1}$.

:::

::: {.remark .notes}

This version is the Lindeberg--L&eacute;vy CLT;
its proof is beyond these notes' scope
[@billingsley1995probability, Theorem 27.1].
Other versions relax the IID assumption,
which is why the informal statement asks only that no summand dominate.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#cor-clt-sum}
#### Central Limit Theorem for a sum

Let $X_1, X_2, \ldots$ be [IID](independence.qmd#def-iid) random variables
with population mean $\mean$ and finite variance $\ss > 0$,
and let $S_n \eqdef \sumin X_i$.
Then for every real number $z$:

$$
\lim_{n \to \infty} \Prf{\frac{S_n - n\mean}{\sdpar\sqrt{n}} \le z} = \normcdf(z)
$$

:::

::: proof

Since $S_n = n\samplemean{X}{n}$,

$$
\frac{S_n - n\mean}{\sdpar\sqrt{n}}
= \frac{n(\samplemean{X}{n} - \mean)}{\sdpar\sqrt{n}}
= \frac{\sqrt{n}\,(\samplemean{X}{n} - \mean)}{\sdpar},
$$

so the event in this corollary is the event in @thm-clt, and the limits agree.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#cor-sum-iid-moments}
#### Mean and variance of a sum of IID random variables

Let $\dsn{X}$ be [IID](independence.qmd#def-iid) random variables,
each discrete or continuous,
with population mean $\mean$ and finite variance $\ss$,
and let $S_n \eqdef \sumin X_i$.
Then, by [linearity of expectation](expectation.qmd#thm-linearity-expectation)
and the [variance of a linear combination](variance-covariance.qmd#thm-var-lincom):

$$
\ba
\E{S_n} &= n\mean \\
\Var{S_n} &= n\ss
\ea
$$

:::

::: proof

For the mean, apply
[linearity of expectation](expectation.qmd#thm-linearity-expectation)
once per added summand:

$$
\ba
\E{S_n}
&= \sumin \E{X_i}
&& \text{(linearity of expectation, applied } n - 1 \text{ times)} \\
&= n\mean
&& \text{(each } X_i \text{ has mean } \mean \text{)}
\ea
$$

For the variance, apply the
[variance of a linear combination](variance-covariance.qmd#thm-var-lincom)
with every $a_i = 1$.
For $i \ne j$, $X_i$ and $X_j$ are independent
(take $A_k = \reals$ for every other $k$ in the
[definition of independence](independence.qmd#def-indpt)),
so $\Cov{X_i, X_j} = 0$ for
[independent summands](variance-covariance.qmd#thm-indpt-uncorrelated);
and $\Cov{X_i, X_i} = \Var{X_i}$
([covariance of a variable with itself](variance-covariance.qmd#lem-cov-xx)):

$$
\ba
\Var{S_n}
&= \sumin \sumn{j} \Cov{X_i, X_j}
&& \text{(variance of a linear combination, all } a_i = 1 \text{)} \\
&= \sumin \Cov{X_i, X_i} + \sum_{\substack{i, j = 1 \\ i \ne j}}^n \Cov{X_i, X_j}
&& \text{(split off the terms with } i = j \text{)} \\
&= \sumin \Var{X_i} + 0
&& \text{(covariance with itself; independent summands)} \\
&= n\ss
&& \text{(each } X_i \text{ has variance } \ss \text{)}
\ea
$$

:::

::: {.remark .notes}

@cor-sum-iid-moments follows from the two results named in its statement.
It does not depend on @thm-clt or @cor-clt-sum;
@cor-clt-sum centers and scales $S_n$
using the values $n\mean$ and $\sqrt{n\ss}$ from this corollary.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#cor-mean-iid-moments}
#### Mean and variance of a sample mean of IID random variables

Let $\dsn{X}$ be [IID](independence.qmd#def-iid)
[random variables](random-variables.qmd#def-random-variable),
each [discrete](random-variables.qmd#def-discrete-rv)
or [continuous](random-variables.qmd#def-continuous-rv),
with [population mean](expectation.qmd#def-expectation) $\mean$
and finite [variance](variance-covariance.qmd#def-variance) $\ss$,
and let $\samplemean{X}{n} \eqdef \avgin X_i$.
Then:

$$
\ba
\E{\samplemean{X}{n}} &= \mean \\
\Var{\samplemean{X}{n}} &= \frac{\ss}{n}
\ea
$$

:::

::: proof

Let $S_n \eqdef \sumin X_i$, so $\samplemean{X}{n} = S_n / n$.
By @cor-sum-iid-moments, $\E{S_n} = n\mean$ and $\Var{S_n} = n\ss$:

$$
\ba
\E{\samplemean{X}{n}}
&= \frac{1}{n}\E{S_n}
&& \text{(linearity of expectation)}\\
&= \frac{1}{n} \cdot n\mean
&& \text{(mean of a sum of IID variables)}\\
&= \mean
&& \text{(cancel $n$)}\\
\Var{\samplemean{X}{n}}
&= \frac{1}{n^2}\Var{S_n}
&& \text{(variance of a constant multiple)}\\
&= \frac{1}{n^2} \cdot n\ss
&& \text{(variance of a sum of IID variables)}\\
&= \frac{\ss}{n}
&& \text{(cancel one factor of $n$)}
\ea
$$

:::

::: {.remark .notes}

In practice, @thm-clt justifies approximating
$\samplemean{X}{n}$ by a normal distribution with mean $\mean$ and variance $\ss/n$,
and @cor-clt-sum justifies approximating
$S_n$ by a normal distribution with mean $n\mean$ and variance $n\ss$.
By @cor-sum-iid-moments, these are exactly the means and variances
of $\samplemean{X}{n} = S_n/n$ and $S_n$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-clt-5d6}
#### The sum of five dice

A single fair die roll has the discrete uniform distribution on $\set{1, \ldots, 6}$,
which is flat, not bell-shaped (@fig-clt-1d6).
Its mean is $\mean = 3.5$,
and its variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\ss &= \sumto{x}{6} (x - 3.5)^2 / 6 \\
&= 35/12.
\end{aligned}
$$

```{r}
#| label: fig-clt-1d6
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of the outcome of one die"
#| code-fold: true
dice_sum_pmf <- function(n_dice) {
  totals <- rowSums(expand.grid(rep(list(1:6), n_dice)))
  probs <- prop.table(table(totals))
  tibble::tibble(total = as.numeric(names(probs)), p = as.vector(probs))
}

dice_plot <-
  ggplot2::ggplot(mapping = ggplot2::aes(x = total, y = p)) +
  ggplot2::xlab("sum of dice (x)") +
  ggplot2::ylab("Probability of outcome, Pr(X=x)") +
  ggplot2::expand_limits(y = 0)

dice_plot + ggplot2::geom_col(data = dice_sum_pmf(1))
```

The sum of five independent rolls, $S_5$, is already close to bell-shaped
(@fig-clt-5d6).

```{r}
#| label: fig-clt-5d6
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of the sum of five dice"
#| code-fold: true
pmf_five_dice <- dice_sum_pmf(5)
dice_plot + ggplot2::geom_col(data = pmf_five_dice)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
p_exact <- sum(pmf_five_dice$p[pmf_five_dice$total <= 15])
p_normal <- pnorm(15.5, mean = 5 * 3.5, sd = sqrt(5 * 35 / 12))
```

For example, the exact probability that five dice total at most 15 is
$\Pr(S_5 \le 15) = `r round(p_exact, 4)`$.
The normal approximation that @cor-clt-sum suggests,
with mean $5 \cd 3.5 = 17.5$ and variance $5 \cd 35/12 \approx 14.58$,
evaluated at $15.5$ to account for $S_5$ taking only integer values,
gives $\normcdf\paren{(15.5 - 17.5)/\sqrt{14.58}} \approx `r round(p_normal, 4)`$.

:::
